summary.text: The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, around 65.5 million years ago, wiped out about three-quarters of the plant and animal species on Earth.
Most scientists think a 10 to 15 km wide asteroid caused it, carving the Chicxulub crater and bringing an impact winter that halted photosynthesis in plants and plankton.
It ended both the Cretaceous and the Mesozoic, and afterwards mammals diversified into new forms such as horses, whales, bats and primates.

facts.label: Species lost
facts.value: About 75% of plant and animal species

facts.label: Crater
facts.value: Chicxulub, 180 km wide, on the Yucatán Peninsula

facts.label: Telltale clue
facts.value: Boundary clay unusually rich in iridium

facts.label: Dinosaur survivors
facts.value: Birds, which gave rise to all modern bird species

items.prompt: Geologists find a thin clay layer, unusually rich in the metal iridium, at the same point in rocks around the world. Why does this hint at an object from space?

options.label: Iridium forms only when lightning strikes clay
Iridium is more common in asteroids than in Earth's crust
Iridium is released whenever large animals die off
Iridium builds up in clay during long ice ages

items.explain: The boundary clay, found worldwide, is unusually rich in iridium, a metal more common in asteroids than in Earth's crust.

items.prompt: After the impact, dust and particles hang in the sky and block sunlight for a long time. Which living things are hit directly?

options.label: Deep burrowing worms that never see daylight
Scavengers that feed on dead animals
Plants and plankton that depend on photosynthesis
Insects that feed on rotting leaves

items.explain: With less solar energy reaching the ground, species that depended on photosynthesis declined or died out, and the food chains built on them suffered.

items.prompt: A small mammal is trying to get through the years after the impact. Which diet gave mammals the best odds?

options.label: Eating insects, worms and snails that feed on dead matter
Eating only the leaves of living plants
Hunting only other large animals for meat
Eating only fresh fruit and seeds

items.explain: Neither strictly plant-eating nor strictly meat-eating mammals seem to have survived; survivors ate insects, worms and snails, which fed on dead plant and animal matter.

items.prompt: Crocodile-like animals living in rivers and lakes came through the extinction far better than many land animals. What protected these freshwater ecosystems?

options.label: The water was deep enough to block the impact's heat
Freshwater animals were all too small to need much food
Rivers and lakes kept growing plants alive through the darkness
Their food webs relied more on dead matter washed in from land

items.explain: Stream and lake ecosystems depended less on living plants and more on detritus washed in from the land, which shielded them.

items.prompt: In the oceans, which kind of animal was more likely to die out?

options.label: Sea-floor animals that eat dead matter settling from above
Open-water swimmers that rely on living phytoplankton
Animals buried in the mud of the sea floor
Bottom dwellers that sometimes feed on detritus

items.explain: Extinction was worse in the water column, whose animals depend almost entirely on living phytoplankton, than on the sea floor, where animals can feed on detritus.

items.prompt: One group of dinosaurs made it through the extinction. Which living animals are their descendants?

options.label: Crocodiles and alligators
Lizards and snakes
All modern birds
Sea turtles

items.explain: The surviving dinosaurs were avians, a few ground and water fowl, which radiated into all modern species of birds.
